item.title: Death toll in Pakistan building collapse rises to 8 with about 10 missing
item.description:
Death toll in Pakistan building collapse rises to 8 with about 10 missing
The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan has risen to eightByThe Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 8:48 AM
KARACHI, Pakistan -- The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan rose to eight Friday after rescuers recovered four more bodies, officials said.
Rescuers are still searching for about 10 people believed trapped beneath the rubble of the building, which collapsed Wednesday in Karachi’s Baloch Colony neighborhood, police official Raja Sarwar said.
Relatives of those still missing were in tears as they prayed for their safety.
On Friday, helmeted rescuers carried a body wrapped in a white covering on a stretcher across a mound of shattered concrete and tangled steel bars. Others were trying to reach into gaps in the wreckage in a congested residential area.

Building collapses are common across Pakistan, where construction standards are often poorly enforced and builders frequently use substandard materials or disregard safety regulations to cut costs. Last month, the roof of a private school collapsed in the northwestern city of Peshawar, killing 34 children and a teacher.

item.title: A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again in 3 weeks
item.description:
A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again in 3 weeks
European Council President António Costa says European Union leaders have failed to agree on the 2028-2034 budgetByLORNE COOK Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 7:23 AM
BRUSSELS -- After struggling to chaperone Europe’s leaders through more than 12 hours of high-stakes budget negotiations, European Council President António Costa faced reporters early Friday with a stark assessment. “We didn’t reach an agreement,” he said.
Government leaders from the 27-nation European Union failed to narrow down the size of the 2028-2034 budget — let alone how it might be used. An important loan for Ukraine was caught up in the wrangling.
The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world’s biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.
Costa said “some member states asked for further reductions" in how much they would have to pay in, according to his latest proposals, while most were "opposed to further cuts, and some even proposed to reverse some cuts.”
It was a day of brinksmanship that saw the leaders playing tough for national audiences.
In three weeks, they will try again. The stakes are high. Elections in some key countries are approaching, and new hardline governments or shaky coalitions could complicate matters further.
In coming days, Costa will draw his conclusions from the summit talks — held in two plenary sessions, several group meetings, and the corridor conversations that typify EU budget negotiations — and consult again with capitals.
Some leaders, notably from countries that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, skipped certain meetings. But Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, was unruffled.
“This is a negotiation process,” he said. “It’s normal that the member states try to defend their own national interests.” ...

item.title: Zelenskyy urges the US to pressure Putin, calling Trump’s 'my friend' remark strange
item.description:
Zelenskyy urges the US to pressure Putin, calling Trump’s 'my friend' remark strange
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expressing frustration with the U.S. approach to Russian leader Vladimir PutinBySAMYA KULLAB Associated Press and ELISE MORTON Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 6:22 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe’s future financial commitments to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Trump calling Putin “my friend” at a recent summit in China as “strange” because the Russian leader is “an aggressor and a killer.”
“He can’t be a friend,” Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to Adolf Hitler being viewed as a friend in World War II.
The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies including Israel.
Zelenskyy’s comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and a U.S. envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a “grandmaster” of politics and weeks after Kushner’s partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a “humanitarian.”

item.title: Houthis report 11 killed, including children, in an airstrike, and other Mideast news
item.description:
Houthis report 11 killed, including children, in an airstrike, and other Mideast news
Houthi rebels say an airstrike in southwestern Yemen has killed at least 11 people, including childrenBySUZAN FRASER Associated Press, MUNIR AHMED Associated Press, and FATMA KHALED Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 6:17 AM
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels report that an air strike in southwestern Yemen has killed at least 11 people, including children.
Meanwhile, Turkish and Saudi officials are heading to Pakistan for a meeting of their defense pact that is expected to discuss Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.
The Houthi-run health ministry said Friday that a strike on a densely populated area in southwestern Yemen killed at least 11 people, including children, the latest attack in the fight between the Iran-backed rebel group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.
Ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said on X that an airstrike hit a cinema building in Turbah city in Taiz province early Friday morning, killing people including children who sold ice cream in the area and had been living in part of the building. Al-Asbahi didn’t provide details of how many children were killed and said the death toll was preliminary as rescuers are trying to pull out more bodies from under the rubble.
He blamed the strike on Saudi Arabia. The AP couldn’t independently verify his claims and the Saudi coalition made no public comment about this incident.
Footage aired by Houthi-controlled al-Masirah TV showed a destroyed building and people digging through the rubble to recover the bodies of several children. The AP couldn’t independently verify the footage.
Turkish and Saudi delegations were arriving in Pakistan for talks under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all three countries, security officials said.

item.title: UN warns hunger will deepen in the Middle East
item.description:
UN warns hunger will deepen in the Middle East
Hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with Sudan and Yemen among five nations at the highest level of concern, the U.N.’s food agencies warned FridayByHAMZA FAHMY Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 4:54 AM
CAIRO -- Hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with war-torn Sudan and Yemen among five nations facing the gravest risk, the United Nations’ food agencies warned Friday. The agencies pointed to conflict, soaring fuel costs linked to war in the Middle East and steep cuts in aid.
The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program's Hunger Hotspots report covers December through May 2026.
It places Sudan, Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northern Nigeria at the highest level of concern. All five have appeared on the list repeatedly since 2022. The Palestinian territories were moved down one level following the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, though 67% of Gaza’s population still faces crisis-level hunger or worse, and the report warned that the gains were fragile.
In Sudan, a risk of famine is expected to persist through January in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan, the report said. Nearly 19.5 million people, or 41% of the population, faced crisis-level hunger or worse in the latest nationwide analysis. In two displacement camps in South Darfur’s Eastern Jebel Marra, acute malnutrition rates exceeded the threshold for famine.
Sorghum prices in Sudan more than doubled in a year, driven by the fighting and by higher fuel costs tied to the Middle East conflict. Diesel prices have also more than doubled from a year earlier because of the Middle East conflict, according to the report.
Drought linked to El Niño — a natural warming of Pacific Ocean water that disrupts weather worldwide — has added to the strain, affecting up to 55% of cropland in Sennar state and 70% in Gedaref, two of Sudan’s main farming states.

item.title: Pakistan set to host talks with Saudi Arabia and Turkey under trilateral defense pact
item.description:
Pakistan set to host talks with Saudi Arabia and Turkey under trilateral defense pact
Officials say Pakistan is set to host talks with Saudi Arabia and Turkey under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all threeByMUNIR AHMED Associated Press and SUZAN FRASER Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 2:55 AM
ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan is set to host talks Friday with Saudi Arabia and Turkey under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all three, two security officials said.
The talks in Islamabad will focus on developments in the Middle East, including ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels, the officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the meeting publicly.
They said delegations from Turkey and Saudi Arabia have started arriving in the capital.
Meanwhile, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan formally approved the three-nation agreement, completing Turkey’s ratification process for the defense pact, according to Turkey’s Official Gazette on Friday.
Earlier this month, legislators approved the agreement by 279 votes to 119 in Turkey’s 699-seat parliament, despite objections from opposition parties who had argued that the agreement could embroil Turkey in regional wars and put Turkish soldiers in harm’s way.
Turkish officials have said Ankara is considering sending military assistance to Saudi Arabia but insist that the Mecca agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops would be deployed to fight in Yemen or to attack the Houthis.
Pakistan has said that the agreement is purely defensive in nature and it is not against anyone, including Iran, and that the trilateral alliance reflects a shared desire to strengthen strategic security cooperation.
Senior diplomats as well as defense and military officials from the three countries are expected to discuss ways to deter threats, expand military cooperation...

item.title: UN peacekeepers are preparing to leave southern Lebanon. There’s no plan for what comes next
item.description:
UN peacekeepers are preparing to leave southern Lebanon. There’s no plan for what comes next
The U.N. peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon is preparing to end a 50-year mission as tensions between Israel and Hezbollah remain highByABSEWELL Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 12:15 AM
Share
NAQOURA, Lebanon -- Among the few buildings still standing in the Lebanese border town of Naqoura are an abandoned hotel occupied by Israeli soldiers, its walls draped with anti-drone netting, and the compound housing the headquarters of the U.N. peacekeeping force.
The roads passing through the once-idyllic seaside town, now largely reduced to rubble, are empty except for the occasional military patrol or convoy of peacekeepers escorting civilians or supplies.
The end of the nearly 50-year mandate of the UNIFIL peacekeeping force is looming in just over a month, and still there is no plan for what comes after it.
The peacekeepers' impending exit, in parallel with an ongoing occupation by Israeli forces and a debate over the disarmament of the Hezbollah militant group, leaves the future of southern Lebanon in limbo.
Lebanon wants the U.N. force to stay. But the U.N. Security Council voted last year to terminate UNIFIL’s mandate at the end of 2026, bowing to demands from the United States and its close ally Israel.
Israel says the mission was a failure, citing Hezbollah’s military buildup over the years. The peacekeepers say they helped preserve calm for 17 years before Hamas’ 2023 attack on southern Israel ignited a regional conflict.
“My mandate is not to disarm Hezbollah,” UNIFIL’s commander, Maj. Gen. Diodato Abagnara, told The Associated Press in an interview. “My mandate is to support the Lebanese Armed Forces, to create the best conditions for the Lebanese Armed Forces to take full control here in the south. It’s not to fight against Hezbollah.”
UNIFIL is set to begin a gradual drawdown of its 7,500 peacekeepers on Jan. 1. Whatever comes after that, he said...

item.title: South Korea lets a North Korean fisherman resettle in South and returns six others
item.description:
South Korea lets a North Korean fisherman resettle in South and returns six others
Seoul says that one of seven North Koreans rescued off a fishing boat drifting near a South Korean island earlier this month chose to resettle in the SouthByHYUNG-JIN KIM Associated PressNovember 26, 2026, 11:19 PM
Share
SEOUL, South Korea -- Seoul said Friday that one of seven North Koreans rescued off a fishing boat drifting near a South Korean island earlier this month chose to resettle in the South.
South Korea's Unification Ministry said it let the six others return to North Korea aboard their boat across the Koreas’ eastern maritime border Friday morning.
The North Koreans were rescued by South Korea's navy and coast guard in international waters near South Korea's eastern Ulleung Island on Nov. 3.
It's not uncommon for North Korean fishing boats to be found adrift south of the Koreas' eastern and western sea boundaries. South Korea typically returns North Korean fishermen if they want to go home and are not suspected of espionage. But South Korea lets them resettle in the South if they so choose.

item.title: What to know about North Korean move to shut down Swiss diplomatic office
item.description:
What to know about North Korean move to shut down Swiss diplomatic office
North Korea has shut down a Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang and expelled its head, signaling a more assertive foreign policyByKIM TONG-HYUNG Associated Press and HYUNG-JIN KIM Associated PressNovember 26, 2026, 10:46 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
SEOUL, South Korea -- In shutting down a month-old Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang and expelling its head, North Korea has signaled it will set its own terms as it pursues a more assertive foreign policy. But experts say the move could potentially risk the loss of many European nations as alternative diplomatic partners.
The Swiss drew the anger of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un after they imposed sanctions on a youth camp over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
Just a few days earlier, in a more upbeat diplomatic moment, Kim received credentials from 10 newly appointed ambassadors, including envoys from ally Russia and longtime diplomatic partner Sweden, in the first such event of his 15-year rule.
Kim used the meeting with ambassadors to defend his nuclear arms buildup and call for the world to respect North Korea’s sovereignty, a standard Pyongyang later accused Switzerland of failing to meet by sanctioning the camp.
Here's a look at the closure of the Swiss office in Pyongyang and what it says about North Korea’s foreign policy.
North Korea’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday summoned Sylvain Astier, head of the Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, declared him persona non grata and handed him a notice demanding the office’s closure and his departure from the country within 48 hours.
